source: Gerwig et al. (2021) The relationship between intelligence and divergent thinking: a meta-analytic update
finding: Three-level meta-analysis. DT and intelligence correlate modestly. The rise over Kim (2005) is mostly due to correcting for measurement error.
numbers: r = .25, 95% CI [.21,.30]; 112 studies, 849 correlations, N = 34,610; I2 = 92%; difference prior-Kim vs post-Kim not significant
limits: Very high heterogeneity. Funnel plot asymmetric; trim-and-fill imputed 169 coefficients on the high-effect side.
agent_relevance: DT is not a proxy for general reasoning ability. An open-mode metric for the agent should be validated separately from accuracy on closed tasks.

source: Gerwig et al. (2021) The relationship between intelligence and divergent thinking: a meta-analytic update
finding: Scoring method moderates the link. Fluency alone relates least to intelligence. Originality-type scores relate more.
numbers: fluency r = .20; composite score r = .37; fluency vs originality contrast z = -3.75, p < .001; QM(2) = 22.47
limits: The composite result was not robust to sensitivity checks (confounded with other moderators).
agent_relevance: Counting ideas (fluency) and judging idea quality measure different things. The agent needs a quality score next to a count.

source: Gerwig et al. (2021) The relationship between intelligence and divergent thinking: a meta-analytic update
finding: Instructions moderate the link. Game-like instructions gave no significant DT-intelligence correlation. Test-like and strategy instructions gave small to moderate correlations. Best fit: be-creative instruction scored for originality.
numbers: QM(2) = 25.94, p < .001 (test-like vs game-like z = -4.94); instruction-by-scoring fit chi2(1) = 6.70, p = .010; highest r about .31-.37 for be-creative plus originality; facet (g, gf, gc) r = .23-.28, QM(2) = 5.77, p = .056
limits: Most studies used be-fluent instructions (59 studies). Time-condition effects were confounded with publication year.
agent_relevance: Task framing changes what the metric measures. Report the prompt framing with every open-mode score.

source: Gerwig et al. (2021) The relationship between intelligence and divergent thinking: a meta-analytic update
finding: Sample moderators: the correlation rose with mean sample age and fell as the share of women rose. The threshold question was not tested at effect-size level because of method problems.
numbers: age: positive association; percent female: negative association (exact slopes in paper, not recorded)
limits: Moderators are correlational and tangled with year of publication.
agent_relevance: Little direct use; shows that DT validity is sample-dependent.

source: Weiss et al. (2020) A reappraisal of the threshold hypothesis of creativity and intelligence
finding: Two large studies using three continuous methods (scatterplot and heteroscedasticity, segmented regression, local structural equation models) found no threshold in the DT-intelligence relation. The authors call for dropping the threshold hypothesis.
numbers: N1 = 456, N2 = 438; DT-intelligence r = .19 (study 1) and r = .27 (study 2); no significant slope change at any breakpoint
quote: we recommend the total abandonment of the threshold
limits: German-language samples; DT measured by AUT items (study 1) and six verbal and figural tests (study 2). A failed test of an old claim, not proof for every population.
agent_relevance: The belief that only high-ability thinkers benefit from open-mode generation lacks support. Do not gate divergent generation on a capability estimate.

source: Barbot, Van den Noortgate, Said-Metwaly (2026) Robust but tiny: the serial order effect in creativity
finding: The serial order effect (later ideas are more original) shows at group level but is small and depends on task and scoring. Individual slopes are not stable.
numbers: 4,752 responses to three AUT prompts; Cohen's d = 0.31 (subjective), 0.38 (frequency), 0.06 (semantic similarity); variance explained at most 3.5%; ICCs of slopes below .31 across prompts
quote: the SOE appears robust at the group level yet unreliable in terms of inter-individual stability
limits: One dataset (German sample, 2.5 min limit). Shorter sequences reduce slope reliability.
agent_relevance: The 'push past the obvious ideas' rule has a real but small basis. Use it as a mild prior, not a core mechanism.

source: Barbot et al. (2026), citing Gonthier and Besancon (2024) and Miroshnik and Shcherbakova (2019)
finding: Competing account: the serial order effect depends on how long the ideation sequence is. Low-fluency people give more original ideas at any position. High-fluency people show a stronger rise.
numbers: Miroshnik and Shcherbakova: linear R2 = .009 (self-rated) and .008 (expert); quadratic R2 = .038 and .022
limits: Secondhand through the 2026 paper; the cited papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: Idea quality depends on sequence length. Fixed budgets of ideas per prompt will change the metric.

source: Beaty and Johnson (2021) Automating creativity assessment with SemDis
finding: Semantic distance from text models agrees strongly with human creativity ratings when a multiplicative composition model is used. Agreement is weaker in other studies of the paper.
numbers: Study 1 (N = 171): latent r = .91 with human ratings (83% variance), five semantic models; a later study latent r = .45; semantic distance with Gf r about .24, similar to human ratings in Beaty and Silvia 2012 (r = .26)
limits: Additive models penalise longer answers; the multiplicative model reverses that. English, short responses.
agent_relevance: Cheap, repeatable originality score usable inside the agent loop. Needs a length check, because elaboration inflates it.

source: Beaty and Johnson (2021) SemDis, external validity
finding: Latent semantic distance relates to creative behaviour and openness much as human ratings do, but links are moderate.
numbers: Convergent validity with creative-behaviour latent variables; correlations about .2 to .45 across studies (see paper tables)
limits: Only headline latent values recorded here.
agent_relevance: Semantic distance is a proxy, not ground truth. Pair it with a quality or usefulness judge.

source: Haase and Hanel (2023) Artificial muses: generative AI chatbots have risen to human-level creativity
finding: On the AUT, chatbots matched average human originality. Many individual humans still beat the best chatbot.
numbers: 100 humans vs 5 chatbots (plus GPT-4 later), 5 prompts; mixed model B = -0.21, SE 0.15, p = .218 (human raters), B = -0.18, p = .241 (AI raters); on average 32.8 humans beat the best of the five chatbots; 9.4 humans beat GPT-4; rater ICC .85-.94; human-AI scorer r = .78-.94
limits: Chatbots were prompted several times and made 2-3 times more ideas. Fluency and originality were unrelated (r = -.28 to .26). GPT-4 was scored by the AI only. AUT objects likely in training data.
agent_relevance: Fluency is cheap for a model; the question is the best-of-set and diversity, not the mean.

source: Hubert, Awa, Zabelina (2024) The current state of AI generative language models is more creative than humans on divergent thinking tasks
finding: GPT-4 beat 151 humans on three DT tasks by semantic distance, with fluency matched.
numbers: N = 151 humans; AUT group effect F(1,600) = 622.10, eta2 = .51; DAT: GPT 84.56 (SD 3.05) vs humans 76.95 (SD 6.13), t(300) = 13.65; elaboration 38.69 vs 5.45 words; fluency equal (6.94 vs 7.01)
limits: Reported F values for AUT and Consequences are identical in the text (possible copy error). Semantic distance rewards long answers. No usefulness rating. The 2026 review puts the AUT effect at Hedges g = 2.61 and calls it an upper bound.
agent_relevance: Large wins on semantic distance may be a metric artefact. Do not accept a single automated originality score as proof of better thinking.

source: Koivisto and Grassini (2023) Best humans still outperform AI in a creative divergent thinking task
finding: Chatbots beat the average human on the AUT. The best human ideas matched or beat the best AI ideas.
numbers: 256 humans vs ChatGPT3, ChatGPT4, Copy.Ai (11 sessions each, 4 objects); semantic distance mean B = 0.049, SE 0.010, t(274) = 4.949; max scores B = 0.027, p = .003; semantic distance vs human rating r = .55 [.46,.62]; AI held the top semantic-distance score in 1 case and the top human-rating score in 2 cases
limits: 30 s per object, quality-over-quantity instruction. Humans' lowest scores drive the gap. Max-score group differences were not significant in post-hoc tests.
agent_relevance: A model raises the average; the ceiling did not rise. For discovery the tail of the idea distribution is what matters.

source: Evaluation of Large Language Models as Tools, Models, and Partners in Creative Thinking Research (2026 review, GCA framework)
finding: Across independent comparisons LLMs exceed average human DT originality, but the size depends on how fluency was controlled. At the top of the human distribution humans win.
numbers: Hedges g: Hubert AUT 2.61 [2.30,2.91] (post hoc fluency matching); Koivisto AUT 0.70 [0.33,1.06] (prospective matching); Bellemare-Pepin DAT 0.52 [0.39,0.64] (503 model responses vs 500 of 100,000 humans); vs top 50% of humans g = -0.88 [-1.01,-0.75]; figural FIQ subjective creativity g = -1.31
limits: Narrative review, no pooled estimate; tasks not commensurate; classic AUT items likely in training data. Bellemare-Pepin is secondhand here.
agent_relevance: Report fluency and compare against strong humans, not the mean.

source: Evaluation of LLMs in Creative Thinking Research (2026 review), contradictions
finding: Three contradictions in the field: fluency dependence, humans ahead at the peak, and AUT scores not predicting other creative tasks.
numbers: Automated scoring: ICC >= .80 and r >= .70 in selected studies; AUT performance does not consistently predict TTCT, story writing or real-world problem solving (Vinchon 2024; Breithaupt 2024)
limits: Narrative selection of studies; cross-language generalisation untested; individual-level use unsupported.
agent_relevance: Do not use one DT task as the only open-mode benchmark. Use several task types.

source: Arora et al. (2025) Generative AI models outperform students on divergent and convergent thinking assessments
finding: ChatGPT-4o, DeepSeek and Gemini beat students on AUT originality and on the Remote Associates Test.
numbers: 46 students; RAT out of 57: humans 19.13 (SD 9.96), ChatGPT 54.96 (0.89), DeepSeek 51.00 (1.59), Gemini 44.93 (1.88); all p < .001; ChatGPT best on AUT median and max originality for tire
limits: Small convenience sample; RAT near ceiling and items probably in training data; authors question validity of such tests for AI.
agent_relevance: DT and RAT tests built for humans saturate for models. Open-mode metrics for the agent need harder, fresh items.

source: Peeperkorn et al. (2024) Is temperature the creativity parameter of large language models?
finding: Higher sampling temperature gives only slightly more novel stories and less coherence. It is not a creativity dial.
numbers: Llama 2-chat stories rated by humans; temperature to novelty beta = .308 (SE .138); temperature to incoherence .240 (SE .122); no link to cohesion or typicality; rater agreement about .64
limits: One model, one story prompt, non-expert raters.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on temperature to get divergence. Use structure such as memory of earlier ideas.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) NoveltyBench: evaluating language models for human-like diversity
finding: 20 leading models give far fewer distinct answers than human writers. Bigger models in a family are often less diverse.
numbers: Many models give fewer than 3 distinct answers in 10 samples at temperature 1; Claude 3, Gemini and GPT-4o score below 4 of 10 on cumulative utility; equivalence classifier agreed with humans 79%; Gemma 2-2B and Llama 3.2-1B among the most diverse
limits: Human baseline was 8 paper authors per prompt, likely a low estimate of human diversity. Classifier is imperfect.
agent_relevance: Directly relevant. Repeated sampling from the same prompt does not diverge.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) NoveltyBench, interventions
finding: Asking for creative outputs (system prompt) or paraphrasing the prompt helps little. Showing the model its previous answers in context (regeneration) lifts diversity to about human level.
numbers: 100 curated prompts, 8 generations, Claude-3 Opus, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Pro; in-context regeneration roughly matched human writers; GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro exceeded human cumulative utility
quote: asking a model for creative outputs does not work very well
limits: Three models and one prompt set. Costs more tokens and is sequential.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence for a memory-of-prior-ideas step in the scaffold.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: the open-ended homogeneity of language models
finding: Within one model, repeated samples are very similar. Across different models, answers are also very similar.
numbers: 26K open-ended queries; 50 samples x 100 queries; at top-p 0.9 and temperature 1.0, 79% of queries have mean pairwise similarity above 0.8 (random pairs 0.1-0.2); min-p at temperature 2: 61.2% of pairs above 0.8; across models similarity 0.71-0.82 (DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82, vs GPT-4o 0.81)
limits: One embedding model (text-embedding-3-small); embedding similarity may overstate sameness of content.
agent_relevance: Ensembling different models does not give independent ideas. Diversity must come from method.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind, judges and reward models
finding: LM judges and reward models agree less with humans when answers are similar in quality or when annotators disagree.
numbers: 31,250 human annotations, 25 annotators per item; Pearson correlations drop on similar-quality and high-disagreement subsets (values in figures, not recorded)
limits: Figures not tabulated in text.
agent_relevance: An LLM judge for open-mode scoring is least reliable exactly where it is most needed.

source: Wenger and Kenett (2025) We're different, we're the same: creative homogeneity across LLMs
finding: Different LLMs answered AUT, DAT and Forward Flow more like each other than humans do. Individually they match or beat humans.
numbers: Table 7 (AUT): individual creativity humans 0.695, LLM baseline 0.711, very-creative prompt 0.754; population variability humans 0.738, LLM baseline 0.459, very creative 0.576; still far below humans (t = 11.1 to 19.1); LLM answers share many more words
limits: Sentence-embedding variability measure; short system prompts; Prolific human data.
agent_relevance: Prompting for creativity raises the mean but leaves diversity well below human groups. Track population diversity as its own metric.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: Blind expert reviewers rated LLM research ideas as more novel than expert human ideas, with weaker feasibility. The agent lacked diversity.
numbers: 79 expert reviewers, 49 ideas per condition; novelty 4.84 (human) vs 5.64 (AI) vs 5.81 (AI reranked by human), p < .05; of 4,000 seed ideas per topic only about 200 were non-duplicates (cosine above 0.8)
limits: Reviewers judge novelty of ideas, not executed results. Authors note novelty judgement is hard even for experts.
agent_relevance: Over-generate and rank works but saturates: duplicates dominate. The rerank step helped.

source: Acar, Runco, Park (2020), via search snippet: explicit-instructions meta-analysis
finding: Snippet only: across 31 studies, instructions stressing creativity or quality improved DT scores beyond quantity instructions.
numbers: g about .24-.27 (from search snippet; not verified)
limits: Not opened. Identity of source inferred.
agent_relevance: If verified, supports be-original instructions for humans; NoveltyBench shows this is weak for LLMs.

source: Divergent thinking and evaluative skill: a meta-analysis (2022), via search snippet
finding: Snippet only: DT correlates weakly with the ability to judge ideas.
numbers: r = .13, 95% CI [.07,.20]; 20 studies, 96 effect sizes, N = 3,019 (snippet; not verified)
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Generation and evaluation are separable skills. Supports separate generate and select stages.

source: Hubert, Awa, Zabelina (2024), DAT vocabulary analysis
finding: GPT-4 won on DAT semantic distance but reused the same words more often. Humans produced more single-occurrence words.
numbers: Overlap of human and GPT-4 DAT words 9.11%; GPT-4 distance 84.56 vs humans 76.95
limits: Describes word use only; no test of whether rare words mean better ideas.
agent_relevance: High distance with low lexical variety is a mode-collapse signal. Measure both distance and repeat rate.
